title: Pharaoh's dreams (Genesis 41:1–40)
hook: seven fat cows, seven thin; Joseph plans for famine

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph in prison: a butler, a baker, and Joseph's one request. Your line was remember me. Did you thank someone you'd been meaning to? Day three hundred seventy.

Two full years go by. Then the most powerful man in Egypt has a bad night. Pharaoh dreams he's standing by the Nile, and seven cows come up out of the river, sleek and fat, and graze in the reeds. Then seven more come up after them, thin and ugly, and the thin cows eat the fat ones, and look just as thin as before. He wakes, falls asleep again, and dreams of seven full ears of grain on one stalk, swallowed by seven thin, scorched ones. In the morning he calls every wise man and magician in Egypt. Nobody can tell him what it means. And the butler, standing there holding the cup, suddenly remembers something.
screen: `SEVEN FAT, SEVEN THIN.` → `NOBODY CAN EXPLAIN IT.` → `THE BUTLER REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: The butler confesses: I remember my faults this day. There was a young Hebrew in prison. Pharaoh sends for Joseph at once. And notice the detail: Joseph shaves, and changes his clothes. The young man who keeps losing his garments gets a new one. Pharaoh says, I hear you can interpret dreams. Joseph's answer, in the King James Bible: "It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace." The same move as in prison. Not me. God. Then he explains. The two dreams are one. Seven good years of harvest are coming, and after them seven years of famine so severe that the good years will be forgotten. And the dream came twice, he says, because God has settled it. But Joseph doesn't stop at explaining. He gives a plan. Find a wise man and set him over the land. During the seven good years, store up a fifth of the harvest, grain in the cities, kept for the famine. Don't spend all of the good years in the good years. Pharaoh looks around his court and says: "Can we find such a one as this is, a man in whom the Spirit of God is?" And he puts Joseph in charge of all Egypt, second only to Pharaoh himself. This morning he was a forgotten prisoner. By the afternoon he runs the country. Christians have read Joseph as a model of faith joined to practical wisdom: he trusts God with the future and still builds the barns. In this chapter, giving God the credit and drawing up a grain plan sit side by side. Joseph does both.
screen: `SHAVED AND NEWLY CLOTHED.` · `IT IS NOT IN ME: GOD WILL ANSWER.` · `SEVEN GOOD YEARS, SEVEN LEAN.` · `STORE A FIFTH FOR THE FAMINE.` · then, large: `A MAN IN WHOM THE SPIRIT OF GOD IS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: save a little for later. Settle, and breathe. Think about what your fat years look like right now: maybe money, maybe energy, maybe time with someone who won't always be around. Then think of a lean year that will likely come: a hard season, a quiet stretch, getting older. What is one small thing you could set aside now? Money, yes, but also patience, friendships, rest. Picture storing it. If you pray, you can ask for wisdom about it. The bell holds the time.
Pharaoh's dreams. Seven fat cows and seven thin, seven full ears and seven scorched: seven years of plenty, then seven of famine.
Your line: plan for the lean years. Today, put a little aside, a few dollars, an hour, a phone call, for a season that will need it. Day three hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Christians often point to Joseph's storehouses when teaching about stewardship and wise planning, and many church food banks and savings programs draw on this story.

original.note: Hebrew spelling of Pharaoh, from an Egyptian phrase meaning great house, first the palace, then the king.

trapdoor: what you thought: Joseph had a talent for reading dreams.
what it means: he gives God the credit, then turns a warning into a plan, and a forgotten prisoner runs Egypt by evening.
what a scholar hears: Pharaoh's dreams are set at the Nile, whose yearly flood decided whether Egypt ate. ancient Egyptian texts also remember famines, though none can be tied to Joseph.
recall: met Jacob at the well with the sheep

notes: 'I remember my faults this day' (41:9) is near-KJV wording given without quotation marks; confirm.
Pharaoh from Egyptian pr-ꜥꜣ, 'great house': standard etymology; confirm.
Trapdoor: Egyptian famine texts exist (e.g. the later Famine Stela) but none can be linked to Joseph; confirm the phrasing is suitably cautious.
'A fifth' from 41:34. 'Second only to Pharaoh' from 41:40.
'By the afternoon he runs the country' is a narrative compression of the same audience; confirm acceptable.
Audit (10% sample): 'no tension between praying and planning' overstated the text, since Joseph is not shown praying in Genesis 41; now 'giving God the credit and drawing up a grain plan'.
